claim: Before you start a domain transfer to Amazon Route 53, the domain must be unlocked at your current registrar, privacy protection must be disabled if it applies, and you must have the valid authorization code from your current registrar.
question: What must you do before transferring a domain name to Route 53?

evidence.quote: Please make sure before you start the transfer process, (1) your domain name is unlocked at your current registrar, (2) you have disabled privacy protection on your domain name (if applicable), and (3) that you have obtained the valid Authorization Code, or “authcode”, from your current registrar which you will need to enter as part of the transfer process.

claim: The FAQ states that each new Amazon Route 53 account is limited to a maximum of 20 domains.
question: How many domains can a new Route 53 account manage according to the FAQ?

qualifiers.condition: FAQ figure for new accounts; compare with the quotas page for the adjustable value

evidence.quote: Each new Amazon Route 53 account is limited to a maximum of 20 domains.

claim: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall lets you quickly deploy DNS protections across all your VPCs, blocking queries for known malicious domains (denylists) and allowing queries for trusted domains (allowlists) when you use the Route 53 Resolver for recursive DNS resolution.
question: What does Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall do?

values.display: block queries made for known malicious domains

qualifiers.scope: VPCs that use the Route 53 Resolver

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall is a feature that allows you to quickly deploy DNS protections across all of your Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs).

The Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall allows you to block queries made for known malicious domains (i.e. create “denylists”) and to allow queries for trusted domains (create “allowlists”) when using the Route 53 Resolver for recursive DNS Resolution.

claim: DNS Firewall comes with AWS Managed Domain Lists that help protect against suspicious domains and Command-and-Control (C&C) bots.
question: What do AWS Managed Domain Lists in DNS Firewall protect against?

evidence.quote: DNS Firewall also comes with AWS Managed Domain Lists that help you protect against suspicious domains and Command-and-Control (C&C) bots.

claim: With strict DNS exfiltration requirements you can create DNS Firewall rules that deny all outbound DNS queries for domains that are not on your approved lists, a walled-garden approach to DNS security.
question: How can DNS Firewall deny every domain except an approved list?

evidence.quote: (1) If you have strict DNS exfiltration requirements and want to deny all outbound DNS queries for domains that aren’t on your lists of approved domains, you can create such rules for a “walled-garden” approach to DNS security.

claim: DNS Firewall is a regional feature; for policy and governance across multiple AWS accounts you should use AWS Firewall Manager.
question: Can DNS Firewall manage security across multiple AWS accounts, and with which tool?

evidence.quote: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall is a regional feature and secures Route 53 Resolver DNS network traffic at an organization and account level.
For maintaining policy and governance across multiple accounts, you should use AWS Firewall Manager.

claim: DNS Firewall pricing is based on the number of domain names stored in the firewall and the number of DNS queries inspected.
question: What is DNS Firewall pricing based on?

values.display: number of domain names stored within your firewall

evidence.quote: Pricing is based on the number of domain names stored within your firewall and the number of DNS queries inspected.

claim: You can log DNS Firewall activity to an Amazon S3 bucket or CloudWatch log groups, and use Amazon Kinesis Firehose to send logs to a third-party provider.
question: Where can DNS Firewall activity be logged?

values.display: Amazon S3 bucket or Amazon CloudWatch log groups

evidence.quote: You can log your DNS Firewall activity to an Amazon S3 bucket or Amazon CloudWatch log groups for further analysis and investigation.
You can also use Amazon Kinesis Firehose to send your logs to a third-party provider.

claim: DNS Firewall and AWS Network Firewall both protect against outbound DNS query threats but for different deployment models: DNS Firewall when you use Amazon Route 53 Resolver for DNS resolution, Network Firewall when you use an external DNS service.
question: How do Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall and AWS Network Firewall differ in protecting against malicious DNS queries?

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall and AWS Network Firewall both offer protection against outbound DNS query threats but for different deployment models.
Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall is designed to deliver granular control to block DNS requests to malicious or compromised domains if you are using Amazon Route 53 Resolver for DNS resolution.
AWS Network Firewall offers similar capabilities to filter/block outbound DNS queries to known malicious domains if you are using an external DNS service to resolve DNS requests.

claim: Route 53 Profiles let you combine private hosted zone associations, Resolver rules and DNS Firewall rule groups in one RAM-shareable configuration that you can share across accounts and associate with VPCs.
question: What are Route 53 Profiles?

evidence.quote: With Profiles, you can combine various configurations such as private hosted zone (PHZ) associations, Resolver rules, and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule groups within one RAM-shareable configuration.

By sharing the Profile across AWS accounts and associating it with the Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), you have an easy way to ensure that all VPCs have the same DNS configuration without the complexity of managing separate resources.

claim: Route 53 Profiles integrate natively with AWS RAM, so you can share Profiles across accounts or with an AWS Organization, and RAM managed permissions let you attach different permissions to each resource.
question: Are Route 53 Profiles integrated with AWS RAM, and can you restrict who can modify them?

evidence.quote: Route 53 Profiles natively integrates with AWS RAM allowing you to share Profiles across accounts or with an AWS Organization.
Route 53 Profiles utilizes RAM managed permissions which allow users to attach different permissions to each resource.

claim: You can associate up to 5,000 VPCs to a single Route 53 Profile.
question: How many VPCs can be associated with a single Route 53 Profile?

qualifiers.condition: FAQ figure; compare with the quotas page

evidence.quote: You can associate up to 5,000 VPCs to a single Route 53 Profile.

claim: You can create one or more Profiles per account, but you can associate only one Profile per VPC at a time.
question: Can you create more than one Route 53 Profile per account, and how many can a VPC use?

values.display: only associate one Profile per VPC at a time

evidence.quote: Yes, you can create one or more Profiles per account.
However, you can only associate one Profile per VPC at a time.

claim: Route 53 Profiles support private hosted zones and their settings, Route 53 Resolver rules (forwarding and system), and DNS Firewall rule groups.
question: What Route 53 resources can you manage with Profiles?

values.display: private hosted zones and the settings specified within them

evidence.quote: Route 53 Profiles support private hosted zones and the settings specified within them, Route 53 Resolver rules (both forwarding and system), and DNS Firewall rule groups.

claim: You cannot share a Route 53 Profile across AWS Regions.
question: Can a Route 53 Profile be shared across AWS Regions?

values.display: cannot share a Profile across AWS Regions

evidence.quote: No, you cannot share a Profile across AWS Regions
